doc.title: Plas Johnson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

title: Learning licks and listening to the great players
summary: Self-taught by copying players, he advocates collecting and practicing licks, and urges young tenor players to listen to Webster, Jacquet, Young, Byas and Ammons.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: It’s a revelation to me, but that’s not what the book is, the book is about licks. I’m self taught and when I think back over it my first experience with playing when I didn’t know how to play or what to play was listening to other players play and copying, copying what they play or trying to mimic what they play. And it does turn out to be licks, like a study of blues playing, it’s like licks. You can’t say well it’s just three chord changes. You know better. It’s licks, a little two-bar, one-bar, four-bar phrases that you can intertwine in different ways. And if you are a practicing player then you get to try out things that you think work. And if not then you should practice them. You should collect them and practice them. And the more licks you have in your pockets, you know major ninth licks, major seven licks, 2-5 licks, 2-5-1 licks, 3-6, 3-6-2-5. And actually these are little melodies that fit over those chord changes. And you know when young players are coming up to play and they know their harmony on the instrument and everything, well the next step is how do you apply it? So you see the chord changes. They say well I have the chord changes, but you know, what do you play, what do you play when you see such-and-such chord changes. And knowing the licks that fit over these chord changes will help you put some kind of a solo together. And the next alternative is to take the tune and listen to a developed player, what he does on that tune, and study it, and learn it, note for note. And when I talk to players, like Ricky, you know Ricky is a player that came up the same way and we were talking about that last night. He just studied players. When you’re learning to play you study players who you want to sound like and who you think swings pretty good. And your style is how you interpret what you pick up from the players and how you put it together.
Usually there’s one or two people that will speak to you I think, you know?

But the more the merrier. Because there’s a lot of great players. You know you’ve got, my biggest complaint out there is young players they exclude so many of the great players of the past and if you’re playing tenor saxophone he should hear Ben Webster or Illinois Jacquet, Lester Young, Don Byas, Gene Ammons. None of these players should be excluded from your listening habits.
